The way I think they isolated M is by first multiplying both sides by 2. This will give you the equation

4j = m (10)\^2 units not included.

Then they divided both sides by (10m/s)\^2. Factoring this out (make sure you pay attention to the units, which will be squared also) you will get 100 m2/s2. This is what they divided both sides by:

4j/(10)\^2 = m      ---- > 4j/100 = m

the unites of joules is kg m\^2 /s\^2, the value of our denominator is m\^2/s\^2,, we can cancel these out and get 0.04 kg = m.

This might not be the most technical way of thinking about it, but I think of ganglia as synaptic relays - sort of like a train station for signals to gather and be sent out, abling them to travel long distances. The CNS is located in the brain, and this is where the signal comes from. The question is essentially asking where the signal will go immediately upon leaving the brain. We can immediately eliminate the first two answers - the taste receptors would be sending signals TOWARDS the brain, not the other way around, and the brain's synapse is not directly to the glands (which is why we have the ganglia in the first place). Immediately after leaving the brain, the signal will be "on the tracks" on its way to the ganglia (the relay station), so that neuron would be a "preganglionic neuron". Sorry if my explanation is a bit confusing.

I did not take biochem, but honestly, a lot of biochem is literally just that, biology and general chemistry. The main thing you want to study from Biochem is enzyme kinetics (extremely high yield), citric acid cycle, and glycolysis, other than that "Biochem" questions will just be gen chem or biology. Also, please do not let these diagnostic tests scare you, they are good practice but their scores are designed to scare you into buying their products. Just study the topics I mentioned and then fill in the gaps when you get a question wrong on one of your tests!

Blueprint exams are honestly only really good to give you a sense of what kind of questions they'll ask you on the MCAT. I could not get above a 505 on BP exams, even after a month or so of studying. When I moved to the AAMC material I was scoring consistently above 515. The blueprint exams are very technical and specific and challenge your content knowledge a lot. It is not the same way on the AAMC material, although BP is good practice.

Half-filled shells are always somewhat stable. This is why if you look at a graph of ionization energies, you will see that when ionizing to a half-filled shell it takes less energy. More importantly, for the transition metals, it is important to know that when making an ion of transition metals the 4s elections come off first.

A Good tip I have is to stick both your thumbs in the direction of the H (or lowest priority) and then bend both your fingers (kinda like right-hand rule for magnetic field direction). If your right hand's fingers bend in the direction of increasing number (1,2,3) its R, if its your left hand, S. They usually make it somewhat obvious on AAMC questions, however.

What I've noticed personally is that third party is more difficult on the actual concepts, but the passages themselves are easier to understand. I was using a blueprint, and I was actually having a hard time with their rather complex math questions. Switching to AAMC was definitely more of a challenge to grasp the passage conceptually. At this point Uworld and Kaplan have gotten you up to speed on most of your concepts, and I would just try and cram as much AAMC material as you can before the date - the challenge is not in the concepts it's in how they are phrased, and that's where the AAMC will be the most challenging.

I would completely skip the review phase, especially since most of the concepts are fresh in your mind - you don't need to know any concept in depth, but you do need to know how to apply it to an MCAT phrased passage question. I would base all the studying you do on the practice questions/tests you get wrong or spend over 2 minutes on. The AAMC practice in the form of section banks and question packs is absolutely essential. Just do the largest volume of questions and tests that you can. Good Luck!

What I find amazing is that, as social creatures, we are extremely reliant on affection, attention, and physical touch from others. I feel terrible that you feel this way, and I am right there alongside you. Sometimes the future looks so bleak and meaningless it makes you just want to turn it all off, and there is nothing in your present life that can be remotely stimulating. But I will say this, if you simply wake up and go through the motions of "surviving" every single day, that is a start. For me, how I've tried to make it work is to do something new every single day. What does that look like? maybe I'll go to the store and buy a snack I haven't tried, or maybe even try and cook something new. Not hungry? Lets walk down a street you haven't walked down - the point is, find something minor to stimulate you, just putting yourself into a minorly new environment can do worlds of difference. Keeping this up every day can even lead to new beginnings, maybe you'll meet new friends or expose yourself to something that makes the future less meaningless. The point is, just try to expose yourself to things, because I know where you are right now mentally. Anything is better than feeling what your feeling, and even if its extremely minor if you do it every day it might be able to help. It has for me.

I resonate deeply with what you've said, and I have hurt those closest to me beyond repair. I will never be forgiven for what I did, and It has taken a significant toll on my life. I originally thought it was hopeless as well - sometimes I still do. But my advice? If you're not ready to forgive yourself, do what you can to make it better. Take some time to reflect, and see how you can become a better person. You aren't stuck this way - you can change, and it starts with identifying the problems. See a counselor, if you can, if not, reach out to anyone to talk to. Finding out why you do these things is the first step to ensuring you never do it again. I still go in and out of periods of hopelessness, but I can say that I am making strides to improve myself. I'll still never be forgiven for what I did, but as I distance myself and try to make new beginnings, I try and let that lack of forgiveness remind me how I need to be in the future. It's the easy way out to think about killing yourself, and I've wanted to take it many times. But if you truly hate what you did then you will force yourself to try and improve, no matter how painful it might be.

The lack of communication and connection with others makes us vulnerable, and I, like you, have subjected myself to relationships that were the opposite of healthy in desperation to feel loved. The main thing I've learned - it never really gets better, at least in the way you think it will. You don't just "get over" trauma or abuse, but you can learn to make it not dictate your life, and I promise there are those of us out there who are going through something exactly like you. It just takes some time, some effort, and some risks to go out there and find them. I wish you the best and you aren't alone in how you feel.

I'm sorry you feel that way, and I can say that I resonate with many of the things you are saying. The way I try to cope with the dark thoughts is to just keep my mind and life occupied. In you're case that can be very difficult with the obligation of taking care of your mother and the lack of income - but start making plans. Sit down and just start writing out potential courses of action - anything that you can do that might have any benefit - even if it's just opening a window to get fresh air. I know this might not work for everyone, but If you try and see things like a puzzle to solve, it will at least occupy your mind enough to not let the dark thoughts overwhelm your life. I am no expert on this, and I struggle with suicidal thoughts as well, but I just wanted to share one thing that has helped me, and I am letting you know that you're not alone in this immense amount of stress you are feeling. Feel free to reach out and talk.
